title: Space Weather - What's That?!
summary: Josh and Chuck revisit the Sun with a focused episode on space weather, centering on solar flares and how they relate to coronal mass ejections and geomagnetic storms. They cover sunspots and the roughly eleven-year solar cycle, magnetic reconnection, the flare classification scale (A, B, C, M, X), and the Halloween Storms of 2003. They explain how coronal mass ejections interact with Earth's magnetosphere and ionosphere to produce auroras. The Carrington Event of 1859 is covered in detail, including the telegraph disruptions, followed by modern vulnerabilities such as grounding, power grid transformers, GPS, aviation radio, satellites, and astronauts. The episode closes with space weather forecasting and a listener mail segment about Rush fans.

segments.title: Opening banter and space weather introduction
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode as a redo of their earlier Sun episode, with a focus on solar flares as part of space weather, and briefly describe the Sun's plasma and magnetic activity.

segments.title: Solar cycle, sunspots, and magnetic fields
segments.summary: They explain magnetic fields on the Sun, the roughly eleven-year solar cycle and solar maximum, and sunspots, which are cooler, magnetically strong dark spots that can be as wide as Neptune.

segments.title: Solar flares, magnetic reconnection, and flare classification
segments.summary: Solar flares are described as bursts caused by magnetic field lines interacting, with magnetic reconnection proposed to explain their fast energy release. The flares are classified A, B, C, M, and X, each ten times stronger than the last, and the November 2003 flare was estimated around X28 to X45.

segments.title: Coronal mass ejections and Earth's magnetosphere
segments.summary: Coronal mass ejections are described as large eruptions of plasma and charged particles that travel to Earth over about three days. Earth's magnetosphere and ionosphere protect life, and interaction with a CME can produce auroras that appear even near the equator.

segments.title: The Carrington Event of 1859
segments.summary: Richard Carrington observed and sketched a solar flare on September 1, 1859, the first recorded. That night auroras appeared worldwide, and telegraph systems overloaded, sparking, shocking operators, and in one case sending messages with the batteries disconnected.

segments.title: Modern vulnerability: grounding, power grid, and infrastructure
segments.summary: Modern electrical grids use Earth as a ground, and buried metal infrastructure can carry currents induced by a geomagnetic storm, potentially failing transformers. A 1972 solar flare disrupted phone service in Illinois and set off magnetic sea mines in Vietnam. Replacing transformers is costly.

segments.title: Satellites, GPS, aviation, astronauts, and forecasting
segments.summary: Solar storms can disrupt GPS, satellites, and high-frequency aviation radio, and expose astronauts on spacewalks, though the ISS is shielded. The 2003 event disrupted satellites and blacked out a city in Sweden. Ice core nitrate records suggest the Carrington Event is a roughly 500-year event. Space weather forecasters at NOAA and the National Weather Service give about eight to ten minutes of warning.

segments.title: Digression on movies and live shows
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the film Gravity, the movie The Revenant, and anecdotes from a tour show.

segments.title: Listener mail: Rush fans
segments.summary: A listener named Megan writes that her future mother-in-law is a major Rush fan, and mentions the term 'getty corns' for female Rush fans. The hosts respond and thank listeners.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the episode and remind listeners how to send feedback.
